The maximum adult body length achieved by Trumpet emperor in the waters of the Great Barrier Reef is approximately 90 cm [Li = approximately 90 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the genus Lethrinus. This ultimate total length corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of about 10,301 grams (about 10301 grams) [Wwi = about 10301 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for this species. At the other extreme, the wet weight at birth, based on an egg diameter comparable to that of the congener Lethrinus lentjan, is estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], reflecting the tiny, transparent, pelagic eggs that characterize this taxon. These eggs are released into the water column during broadcast spawning events, where fertilization occurs externally. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The pronounced disparity between the miniscule birth mass and the substantial adult weight underscores the extensive scope for somatic growth that defines the species' life-history trajectory.

At a sustained water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 8% [GSI = 8%]. This index was calculated from gravid females collected during the summer spawning season. The total length at which individuals first attain puberty is 36.1 cm [Lp = 36.1 cm], a size threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 251.2 grams [Wwp = 251.2 grams]. Reaching this body size typically requires several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates and small fishes. The onset of gonadal activity at this length marks a critical developmental milestone, after which energy previously channeled entirely into somatic growth becomes increasingly partitioned toward gamete production and reproductive behavior, including the formation of temporary spawning aggregations.

For individuals maintained under stable thermal conditions at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the maximum recorded longevity in wild populations is 9,490 days (9490 days) [am = 9490 days], a lifespan that exceeds that of several sympatric lethrinid species. This considerable longevity is facilitated by a relatively slow pace of life, characterized by moderate growth rates and deferred reproductive maturation. The oldest specimens were identified through otolith increment analysis, which provides reliable age estimates for tropical teleosts. Such extended lifespans imply that sexually mature individuals have multiple opportunities to reproduce across successive spawning seasons, a life-history strategy that buffers population recruitment against years of poor environmental conditions. Indeed, an iteroparous schedule allows older, larger females to contribute disproportionately to the next generation due to their greater fecundity and the production of higher-quality eggs. This demographic pattern is common among large-bodied reef fishes that occupy upper trophic levels.

Comparative studies with other lethrinids reveal that the species attains sexual maturation at a reasonably early point relative to its total growth potential. Data from field surveys indicate that 50 percent of individuals are mature at a total length of 36.1 cm [Lp = 36.1 cm], which is approximately 40 percent of the ultimate total length of 90 cm [Li = 90 cm]. Such a ratio is typical of species that experience moderate fishing pressure and that have evolved to reproduce before the risk of senescence or size-selective mortality becomes substantial. In terms of mass, the transition to the adult phase is marked by a wet weight at puberty of 251.2 grams [Wwp = 251.2 grams], a value that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate potential wet weight of over 10,000 grams. This considerable scope for post-maturation growth allows individuals to continue increasing their reproductive output as they age, since fecundity in teleosts is strongly correlated with body size.

The newly spawned egg has a minute wet weight of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value consistent with the production of small, pelagic propagules that drift with ocean currents during the early larval phase. This dispersal strategy exposes the vulnerable yolk-sac larva and subsequent feeding larva to variable oceanographic conditions, which strongly influence survival rates. Under optimal rearing temperatures near 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the embryonic period is brief, and the prolarva emerges with a modest yolk supply. The gonadosomatic index measured in actively spawning females averaged 8% [GSI = 8%] at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. These life-history attributes, together with a calculated maximum lifespan of approximately 9,490 days (9490 days) [am = 9490 days] under the same thermal regime, portray Trumpet emperor as a K-selected strategist that balances moderate fecundity with extended longevity and multiple reproductive opportunities across its adult life at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C].
